article.overview: A solar telescope is an optical instrument designed to observe the Sun at selected wavelengths in order to study its surface, atmosphere and outer corona. A lunar solar telescope would operate outside Earth's atmosphere, which strongly absorbs ultraviolet radiation [2], and could observe the Sun for long periods from a stable, airless site. This entry describes a payload class rather than one standard instrument. The sources reviewed describe proposals and laboratory-stage designs for lunar solar telescopes; they do not describe a flown lunar instrument dedicated to solar observation. The most detailed concept reviewed is the Lunar Solar Occultation Explorer (LunaSOX), which would use the lunar limb to block the solar disk and image the solar corona [1].
article.description: A solar telescope differs from a conventional astronomical telescope in one important way: the Sun is extremely bright, so the optics, filters and detectors must be designed to select narrow wavelength bands and avoid overwhelming the detector with unwanted light. Two broad approaches appear in the sources reviewed. The first is a conventional telescope with a primary mirror, optical relay and a set of narrow-band filters, which records the Sun at chosen wavelengths. The LunaSOX concept uses this approach with co-aligned filter wheels [1]. The second approach uses the Moon as an occulter. When the Moon's limb covers the solar disk, the instrument can image the much fainter corona around it [1]. A third concept, the lunar-based multi-wavelength telescope described in a 2010 SPIE paper, would combine a reflective telescope with a wavelength-splitting system to observe infrared, visible and ultraviolet bands [2]. Each approach has different requirements for pointing, thermal control, filtering and data handling.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main scientific aim of lunar solar telescopes is to study the Sun's atmosphere, especially the corona, at high resolution and high cadence. The LunaSOX design goals include imaging the corona from about 1 to more than 10 solar radii, at a design target resolution of 0.7 arcseconds [1]. Filter bands proposed for LunaSOX include H-alpha, several iron and nickel coronal emission lines and white light [1]. The UK-led MESOM proposal states that observations of the innermost corona are important for space weather, solar storms and coronal heating [4]. Secondary applications proposed for the LunaSOX concept include measurements of the lunar exosphere, lunar dust and ions, space weather monitoring and a possible lunar relay network [1]. These are proposed applications; none has been demonstrated by a flown lunar instrument in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: In a conventional lunar solar telescope, sunlight enters a telescope such as the Ritchey–Chrétien design proposed for LunaSOX. The optics form an image of the Sun, and filters select the wavelength band to be recorded. The LunaSOX design is a 0.2 m diameter telescope with a focal ratio of f/8.0, and its folded light path resembles that of the LASCO C1 coronagraph, but without an internal occulter or Lyot stop [1]. In the occultation approach, the Moon's limb blocks the bright solar disk. The Sun appears to rise or set at the limb, and the visible part of the corona is recorded as the geometry changes. The LunaSOX paper estimates that the Moon blocks about half the corona in each image, so complete coverage would require mosaics [1]. The orbital and surface cadence therefore depends on the geometry of the lunar orbit or surface site, and the LunaSOX paper gives cadences of 1 to 12 hours for an orbiting platform and about 14 days for a surface site per 180-degree coronal view [1].
article.scientific_importance: The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is far fainter than the solar disk and is normally studied during total solar eclipses on Earth or with coronagraphs in space. LunaSOX proposes to use the Moon itself as the occulter, which would allow coronal imaging at high resolution and cadence over the range of about 1 to 10 solar radii [1]. Its authors argue that dust-scattered light from the lunar surface would be far dimmer than the sky background in Earth-based eclipse observations, although this background level is a design target rather than a measured value [1]. A separate UK-led proposal, MESOM, notes that the innermost corona is important for space weather, solar storms and coronal heating; it is described as a small satellite that uses the Moon's shadow, not as a lunar surface instrument, and its status after its 2025 submission is not confirmed [4]. Lunar-based multi-wavelength instruments would extend observations into infrared, visible and ultraviolet bands from a site without atmospheric absorption [2]. These concepts show scientific value, but none has yet been shown in the sources reviewed to have been built and flown as a lunar solar telescope.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a solar telescope payload. The examples below are one proposed occultation-based telescope, one lunar-based multi-wavelength concept and one flown lunar-surface telescope that was not a solar telescope. They illustrate the range of published information and are not directly comparable. Unless stated otherwise, the values below are design targets rather than measured performance.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No overall dimensions are published for the LunaSOX concept beyond its 0.2 m aperture. The SPIE 2010 concept's dimensions were not verified. The Apollo 16 instrument's dimensions are not stated in the NASA source. Dimensions for any future lunar solar telescope would depend on its aperture, focal ratio, filter system, thermal enclosure and mounting, none of which is fixed by the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass is published for the LunaSOX concept, the SPIE 2010 concept or the Apollo 16 instrument in the sources reviewed. Mass would affect launch requirements, lander capacity and smallsat design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in quantitative terms for any example. The LunaSOX concept is described as using solar power, batteries and, for a smallsat option, electric ion propulsion. The LunaSOX paper notes that ARTEMIS-type batteries (about 4 hours in eclipse) would exceed the roughly 2-hour longest eclipse of that orbit.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar solar telescope would operate in an environment without an atmosphere, with large surface temperature swings and exposure to lunar dust and micrometeoroids. For the LunaSOX concept, lunar dust is the main background concern: the design requires scattered light from dust to remain below the target level so that faint coronal structures can be measured [1]. Operational geometry matters because an orbiting platform in an ARTEMIS-like eccentric orbit could observe daily, with eclipse intervals of up to about 2 hours. The LunaSOX paper notes that the ARTEMIS batteries, at about 4 hours in eclipse, would exceed this longest eclipse [1]. A surface site would observe on a biweekly cadence, because the corona rises or sets over about 4.7 hours near the equator [1]. For a 1-image-per-second campaign over 2 hours of eclipse per day, the LunaSOX paper estimates about 190 GB of data per day, which means data storage and communications would be important design constraints [1].
article.limitations: The main limitation is that the sources reviewed describe proposed and laboratory-stage designs rather than flown lunar solar telescopes. A Moon-based occulter blocks about half of the corona from each image, so complete coverage needs multiple observations [1]. The LunaSOX performance numbers are design targets, and the mass, dimensions and power of the concept are not published in the source [1]. Surface-based observations are much less frequent than orbital ones, with a biweekly cadence for the corona view [1]. The data volume estimate indicates that onboard processing or communications capacity could limit the mission [1].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A solar telescope payload would be integrated on Earth, launched, transferred to the Moon and delivered either by a lander to the surface or by a spacecraft into lunar orbit. No named lander, spacecraft or launch vehicle is verified as compatible with a solar telescope payload.
transportation_process: Integrate the telescope, filter system and thermal enclosure into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it using a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
For a surface telescope, deliver it to the surface with a lander and deploy it on a stable site.
For an orbiting telescope, insert it into lunar orbit, commission its attitude control and thermal systems, and establish its data link.
Verify pointing, thermal and power interfaces before operations begin.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph was set up by a crew member on a tripod in the lunar module's shadow, so it received no direct sunlight during its astronomical observations [3]. A solar telescope would need a different arrangement, because it must point at the Sun and manage intense sunlight. The LunaSOX concept describes a smallsat with solar electric ion propulsion and three-axis attitude control, with a constellation or a larger surface telescope as alternatives. The paper considers an eccentric 1 by 10 Rm lunar orbit modelled on ARTEMIS P1 and P2, and a low circular orbit for hourly cadence [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph is the historical example of a lunar-surface telescope deployed by astronauts; it was not a solar instrument [3]. The LunaSOX paper's timeline lists LOI plus at least 13 years for the mission, which refers to the ARTEMIS reference timeline and is not a confirmed launch date [1].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No named lander, spacecraft or launch vehicle is verified as compatible with a solar telescope payload in the sources reviewed. Compatibility would depend on mass, dimensions, mounting, pointing and thermal requirements, and power and communications interfaces, none of which is published for the LunaSOX concept [1].

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph was the first telescope used to make astronomical observations from the surface of another planetary body, according to NASA [3]. Its work, including imaging Earth's upper atmosphere in ultraviolet light, shows that the lunar surface can host useful astronomical instruments. It was not a solar telescope. Solar observation from the Moon has been proposed in later concepts, including the 2010 SPIE multi-wavelength design [2], the 2023 LunaSOX occultation concept [1] and the 2025 MESOM proposal [4]. These proposals are the main reviewed evidence for the solar telescope payload class.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The main limitations are the lack of flown lunar solar telescope hardware in the sources reviewed, the design-stage status of the LunaSOX parameters (design targets are not measured performance), and the absence of published mass, dimensions, power and lifetime for the LunaSOX concept. The LunaSOX mission duration and launch timing are not confirmed, because the cited timeline refers to the ARTEMIS reference orbit [1]. The SPIE 2010 concept could be described only from a search-result summary, and the full text was not accessed, so its wavelength coverage, optical design and performance are not verified here [2]. The outcome of the MESOM proposal was not found; the most recent source reviewed is a July 2025 press release that states a decision was expected later that year [4]. A Moon-based occulter removes about half of the corona from each image, so full coverage needs mosaics [1]. Several low-quality web pages described a planned lunar solar telescope launch in late 2027 and an Artemis III micro-coronagraph; these claims were not corroborated by NASA, ESA or peer-reviewed sources and are excluded from this article. No direct image asset URL was verified for this payload, so the article contains no embedded images.

data_quality_notes: LunaSOX values (aperture, filter bands, field of view, resolution, integration time, background target) are proposed design parameters from Cooper et al. (2023), not measured performance.
The LunaSOX paper gives no mass, dimensions, power or TRL; these are recorded as null.
The SPIE 2010 entry was taken from a search-result summary; the full text and authors could not be accessed in this session, so its numerical specifications are null.

The Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph is a flown lunar-surface telescope but not a solar telescope; it is included only as a precedent. Its wavelength range is not stated on the NASA source and is recorded as null.
MESOM is a 2025 ESA F-class submission described as a small satellite using the Moon's shadow; the sources do not describe it as a lunar surface instrument, and its selection outcome was not found.

Low-quality web pages claiming a late-2027 Lunar Solar Telescope launch, a first dedicated solar observatory on another body, and an Artemis III micro-coronagraph were not corroborated and are excluded.
No direct image asset URLs were verified for this payload, so no images are embedded.
